proxy_language: Proto-Basque / Early Proto-Vasconic (as a speculative stand-in); fallback to reconstructed Proto-Indo-European is explicitly rejected
proxy_rationale: The Magdalenian (c. 21,000-12,000 BP) predates any possible linguistic reconstruction by many millennia; no language of the culture is known. The only living language isolate in the Franco-Cantabrian heartland is Basque, and some scholars (e.g. Hoz, Trask-style cautious views; Forni 2013 and Gorrochategui/Lakarra on Pre-Basque) argue Basque descends from a pre-Indo-European language of western Europe. Linking it to Magdalenian hunter-gatherers is unprovable and ancestry-based genetic discontinuities (Villalba-Mouco 2019; Posth 2016) make direct continuity doubtful, so Proto-Basque phonotactics (Lakarra's reconstruction) are used only as a defensible, region-appropriate phonological model, not as the Magdalenian language itself. Names should read as plausibly pre-IE western European, not as modern Basque words.
phonology: Modelled on Proto-Basque reconstruction (Michelena 1977, Lakarra 2011): vowels *a *e *i *o *u (five-vowel system, no length contrast). Consonants: stops *p *t *k, *b *d *g (lenis, uncertain for the earliest stage), affricates *ts *tz *tx (apical/laminal/palatal sibilant series), fricatives *s *z *x (sh), *h (late), nasals *m *n *ñ, liquids *l *r (tap) *rr (trill), glide *y. Michelena's reconstructed Proto-Basque has a fortis/lenis stop contrast that is partly secondary. Treat this as an approximation only.
phonotactics: Mostly CV(C) syllables. Onset: single consonant; initial clusters absent in native words (Proto-Basque likely avoided word-initial *r- and many initial clusters; *p *t *k and *b *d *g dominate onsets). Codas: only liquids, nasals, sibilants (-l -n -r -s -z -x), plus stops in compounds. Roots are typically CVC(V) or CVCV, dissyllabic bases most common. Medial clusters limited to nasal/liquid/sibilant + stop (nt, nk, rt, rk, lt, st, tz, ts). Stress and tone not marked in spelling; no diacritics needed.
orthography: Basque-style Latin transliteration: tx = palatal affricate, ts = laminal affricate, tz = apical affricate, x = palatal fricative (sh), z = apical s, s = laminal s, rr = trill, ñ = palatal nasal, h used only rarely. Reconstructions marked with asterisk. Written lowercase; proper names capitalised.
morphology: Agglutinating, suffixing. Nouns take case suffixes (genitive -en/-ko, locative -n/-an, absolutive zero, ergative -k). Definite article -a is a late development. Derivation: -tegi 'place of', -di/-eta 'collective / place with many', -le 'agent/doer', -tu 'verbalizer', -ko 'of/pertaining to', -ar 'inhabitant', -tasun 'abstract', -gabe 'without'. Reduplication occasional in expressive vocabulary (e.g. zirt-zart). Native stem inventory is small and many roots are monosyllabic or disyllabic.
compounding: Compounds are head-final (modifier + head), written together: harri 'stone' + gain 'top' = harrigain. Genitive constructions place possessor before possessed with -en or -ko: X-ko Y or X-en Y 'Y of X'. Agent nouns: object + verbal root + -le ('X-doer'); place nouns: X + -tegi/-eta. Linking vowels are rarely needed; a compound often drops a stem-final vowel or inserts -a-/-e- at the join.
noun_phrase_order: Modifier-head: adjectives follow the noun in modern Basque (etxe handi 'big house'), but compounds and genitives are modifier-head (X-ko Y). For name building use head-final compounds and possessor-before-possessed genitives.
sources: Trask, R. L. (1997) The History of Basque
Lakarra, J. (2011) Ná-De-Ná: Basque historical linguistics essays
Hualde, J. I. & Ortiz de Urbina, J. (eds.) (2003) A Grammar of Basque
Villalba-Mouco, V. et al. (2019) Survival of Late Pleistocene hunter-gatherer ancestry in the Iberian Peninsula (Current Biology)
Glottolog: Basque; Wiktionary: Proto-Basque reconstruction pages
notes: Strictly speculative. Magdalenian groups left no linguistic record, and genetic evidence shows later population turnover in Europe, so Basque-like phonotactics are used only as a plausible aesthetic and structural model for pre-Indo-European western Europe. Do not present these as real Magdalenian words. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word since Magdalenian is not Goidelic; and avoid copying modern Basque words verbatim (e.g. harri, ibai, mendi) unless a deliberate learned-proxy effect is wanted: prefer slightly altered compounds and suffix combinations.
